decks.title: Plant Kingdom — Part 1: Algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes and life cycles
goals: Distinguish green, brown and red algae by pigments and stored food
Describe the features, classes and importance of bryophytes and pteridophytes
Name the three life-cycle patterns and place plant groups in them

slides.heading: Plant Kingdom
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the five groups of plants, then algae, bryophytes and pteridophytes.

visual.alt: Flow of the five plant groups from algae to angiosperms

slides.narration: The plant kingdom ranges from tiny green cells in a pond to giant trees. Biologists arrange plants in five groups: algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms. This part covers the first three, and ends with the life cycles that link all five.

slides.heading: How plants are classified
slides.body_md: Early systems were **artificial**, using a few easy characters. **Natural** systems use many natural affinities, including internal features. **Phylogenetic** systems use **evolutionary relationships**.

rows: Habit, colour, number and shape of leaves; androecium structure

visual.alt: Table of artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems of classification

slides.narration: Artificial systems grouped plants by easy features like habit or leaf shape. Natural systems looked at many characters, including internal structure and chemistry. Modern phylogenetic systems arrange plants by their evolutionary relationships, and newer tools such as numerical taxonomy and chemotaxonomy help.

slides.heading: Algae: body, reproduction and uses
slides.body_md: **Algae** are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and largely aquatic. The body may be **unicellular** (*Chlamydomonas*), **colonial** (*Volvox*), **filamentous** (*Ulothrix*, *Spirogyra*) or **massive** (kelps).

rows: Isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous fusion of gametes

visual.alt: Table of vegetative, asexual and sexual reproduction in algae

slides.narration: Algae live in fresh water, sea water, on moist stones and soil. They fix about half of all the carbon dioxide taken up by photosynthesis on Earth, and add oxygen to their surroundings. Agar comes from red algae, algin from brown algae, and Chlorella and Spirulina are protein-rich food supplements.

slides.heading: Three classes of algae
slides.body_md: Algae are grouped by **pigments**, **stored food** and **cell wall**.

rows: freshwater, brackish water and salt water
cellulose with a gelatinous coating of algin
brackish water and salt water, rarely freshwater
mostly marine, in warmer areas and at great depths

visual.alt: Table comparing green, brown and red algae on pigments, stored food, cell wall, habitat and examples

slides.narration: Green algae have chlorophyll a and b, store starch and have cellulose walls. Brown algae have chlorophyll a and c with the brown pigment fucoxanthin, and store laminarin and mannitol. Red algae carry the red pigment phycoerythrin and store floridean starch; most are marine, some at great depths.

slides.heading: Body of a brown alga
slides.body_md: A large brown alga is anchored by a **holdfast**; the **stipe** supports the leaf-like **frond**. Brown algae have two unequal, lateral flagella on their zoospores.

slides.narration: The holdfast grips a rock under water. Above it the stalk, called the stipe, carries the broad frond, which does the photosynthesis. Examples are Laminaria, Sargassum and Fucus. A gelatinous coat of algin around the cellulose wall helps hold water when the tide goes out.

slides.body_md: Decide the class of an alga from its pigment and food reserve.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which pigment gives brown algae their colour, and what do they store?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: naming the class of an alga
slides.body_md: Three unknown algae are examined. P has chlorophyll b and stores starch; Q has fucoxanthin and stores laminarin; R has r-phycoerythrin and floridean starch. Name each class.
bullets: **P:** chlorophyll b appears only in one class, so **Chlorophyceae** (green).
**Q:** fucoxanthin and laminarin point to **Phaeophyceae** (brown).
**R:** phycoerythrin and floridean starch point to **Rhodophyceae** (red).

visual.alt: Worked table naming the class of each alga from its pigments and food reserve

slides.narration: Pick the clue that is unique. Chlorophyll b belongs only to green algae. Fucoxanthin and laminarin belong to brown algae. Phycoerythrin and floridean starch belong to red algae. One good clue is enough to name the class.

slides.heading: Bryophytes: the amphibians of the plant kingdom
slides.body_md: **Bryophytes** live on land but need **water for fertilisation**. No true roots, stem or leaves; **rhizoids** anchor them. The dominant body is the haploid **gametophyte**; the **sporophyte** depends on it.

rows: Thalloid, dorsiventral, flat on the substrate
Protonema stage, then upright leafy stage
Fragmentation and budding in the protonema

visual.alt: Table comparing liverworts and mosses

slides.narration: Bryophytes are the amphibians of the plant world: they grow on land but need water for the male gamete to swim to the egg. The antheridium makes biflagellate antherozoids and the flask-shaped archegonium makes a single egg. Sphagnum gives peat, and mosses help succession on bare rock.

slides.heading: A moss plant
slides.body_md: The **leafy gametophyte** bears **antheridia and archegonia** at its tip. After fertilisation the zygote grows into a **sporophyte** of **foot, seta and capsule**; meiosis in the capsule makes haploid spores.

slides.narration: The green leafy shoot is the gametophyte, held down by branched threads called rhizoids. The sporophyte grows from its tip. Its foot is embedded in the shoot, a seta lifts the capsule, and spores form in the capsule after meiosis. Each spore grows into a new protonema.

slides.heading: Pteridophytes: first vascular plants
slides.body_md: **Ferns, horsetails and club mosses.** First terrestrial plants with **xylem and phloem**. The main body is the **sporophyte** with true root, stem and leaves; the small free-living gametophyte is the **prothallus**. Water is still needed for fertilisation.

visual.alt: Table of the four classes of pteridophytes with examples

slides.narration: Sporangia sit on leaf-like sporophylls, sometimes packed into cones called strobili. Most pteridophytes are homosporous with one kind of spore. Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous, with large megaspores and small microspores. The female gametophyte keeps the zygote, a first step towards the seed habit.

slides.heading: A fern sporophyte
slides.body_md: The fern **rhizome** bears roots and large **fronds**. **Sori** of sporangia lie on the underside of the **pinnae**; spores germinate into the heart-shaped **prothallus**.

Sori, which are clusters of sporangia, form on the lower surface of the leaflets. Meiosis in sporangia makes the haploid spores that grow into the small prothallus.

slides.heading: Alternation of generations
slides.body_md: A haploid **gametophyte** makes gametes; a diploid **sporophyte** makes spores by meiosis. The two alternate. Three patterns occur: **haplontic**, **diplontic** and **haplo-diplontic**.

rows: all gymnosperms and angiosperms; the alga Fucus
bryophytes and pteridophytes; the algae Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia and kelps

visual.alt: Table of haplontic, diplontic and haplo-diplontic life cycles

slides.narration: In the haplontic pattern the dominant plant is haploid and only the zygote is diploid, as in Spirogyra. In the diplontic pattern the diploid sporophyte dominates, as in seed plants. In the haplo-diplontic pattern both phases are multicellular, as in bryophytes and pteridophytes.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: spore counts and chromosome numbers
slides.body_md: A moss capsule has 40 spore mother cells. Its gametophyte cells have 8 chromosomes. A fern sporophyte has 48 chromosomes in each cell. Find the spores in the capsule, the moss sporophyte number and the prothallus number.
bullets: Each spore mother cell divides by meiosis into 4 spores: $40 \times 4 = 160$ spores.
Moss sporophyte cells are diploid: $2 \times 8 = 16$ chromosomes.
The prothallus is haploid: $48 \div 2 = 24$ chromosomes.

visual.alt: Worked table: 160 spores, 16 chromosomes in the sporophyte, 24 in the prothallus

slides.narration: One diploid spore mother cell gives four haploid spores, so forty cells give one hundred and sixty spores. The sporophyte has double the gametophyte number. The prothallus is haploid, so it has half the sporophyte number.

Algae: green (chlorophyll a and b, starch), brown (fucoxanthin, laminarin and mannitol), red (phycoerythrin, floridean starch).
Bryophytes: liverworts and mosses; dominant gametophyte; sporophyte of foot, seta, capsule.
Pteridophytes: first vascular plants; dominant sporophyte; prothallus; homospory and heterospory.
Life cycles: haplontic, diplontic and haplo-diplontic.

rows: all gymnosperms and angiosperms; the alga Fucus
bryophytes and pteridophytes; the algae Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia and kelps

visual.alt: Table of haplontic, diplontic and haplo-diplontic life cycles

slides.narration: To recap: algae are classified by pigment and stored food. Bryophytes have a dominant gametophyte, pteridophytes a dominant sporophyte with vascular tissue. Life cycles may be haplontic, diplontic or haplo-diplontic, depending on which phase is dominant.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn the **pigment and stored food** of each algal class as a table.
Say **gametophyte** is dominant in bryophytes and **sporophyte** in pteridophytes.
Label **foot, seta and capsule** on a moss sporophyte.
Spore mother cells: **one meiosis gives four spores**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Learn the algal classes as a table of pigments and food. Remember which generation dominates in each group. Label a moss sporophyte correctly. And for spore counts, one meiosis gives four spores.

slides.heading: Seed plants
slides.body_md: Part 2 — plants with seeds: naked seeds, or seeds inside fruits.

visual.alt: Flow showing seed plants divided into gymnosperms and angiosperms

slides.narration: Gymnosperms and angiosperms are the seed plants. In gymnosperms the ovules are not enclosed by an ovary wall, so the seeds are naked. In angiosperms the ovules lie in an ovary that becomes a fruit. This part compares them.

slides.heading: Gymnosperms
slides.body_md: **Gymnos** means naked and **sperma** means seed: the **ovules are not enclosed by an ovary wall**, so seeds stay uncovered. Medium to tall trees and shrubs; *Sequoia* is among the tallest trees.

rows: Tap roots; mycorrhiza in Pinus; coralloid roots with cyanobacteria in Cycas
Simple or compound; needles in conifers

visual.alt: Table of roots, stems, leaves and spores in gymnosperms

slides.narration: Gymnosperms include conifers such as Pinus and Cedrus, and cycads such as Cycas. Roots are tap roots, sometimes with fungi as mycorrhiza or with cyanobacteria in special coralloid roots. Needle shaped leaves, a thick cuticle and sunken stomata reduce water loss in dry or cold conditions.

slides.heading: A cycad: Cycas
slides.body_md: *Cycas* has an **unbranched stem**, **pinnate leaves**, **coralloid roots** that host nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria and **separate male and female plants**.

slides.narration: The unbranched stem carries a crown of large pinnate leaves that last for a few years. The male cone stands at the centre of a male plant. Near the soil surface, small coralloid roots live with nitrogen fixing cyanobacteria, while the tap root goes deeper.

slides.heading: Gymnosperm reproduction
slides.body_md: Male cones bear **microsporophylls** making **pollen grains** (the reduced male gametophyte). Female cones bear **megasporophylls** with **ovules**. The gametophytes stay on the sporophyte, and the seeds are not covered.

nodes.label: Pollen grain = male gametophyte, carried by air
Female cone: ovule with megaspore mother cell
Four megaspores; one becomes the female gametophyte with archegonia
Zygote becomes embryo; ovule becomes a naked seed

visual.alt: Flow of gymnosperm reproduction from male and female cones to a naked seed

slides.narration: Microspores form inside the male cone and develop into pollen grains, a highly reduced male gametophyte. In the ovule one megaspore mother cell divides by meiosis into four megaspores. One grows into the female gametophyte with archegonia. A pollen tube carries the male gametes to the archegonia.

slides.heading: Angiosperms: flowering plants
slides.body_md: **Angiosperms** bear pollen grains and ovules in **flowers**; seeds are enclosed in **fruits**. From *Wolffia*, the smallest, to *Eucalyptus* trees over a hundred metres tall.

visual.alt: Table comparing dicotyledons and monocotyledons

slides.narration: Angiosperms are the dominant land plants and supply food, fodder, fuel and medicines. They fall into two classes. Dicots have seeds with two cotyledons, net veined leaves and flowers with four or five parts. Monocots have one cotyledon, parallel veins and flowers with three parts.

slides.heading: The flower
slides.body_md: The **stamen** (filament and anther with pollen) is the male organ. The **pistil** (stigma, style, ovary with ovules) is the female organ.

slides.narration: The embryo sac forms from a megaspore. Its seven cells are the egg and two synergids, three antipodals, and one large central cell. The central cell has two polar nuclei, which makes eight nuclei in all. The egg apparatus lies at the micropylar end.

slides.heading: Double fertilisation
slides.body_md: A pollen tube releases **two male gametes**. One fuses with the egg (**syngamy**) to form the **zygote**; the other fuses with the **two polar nuclei** (**triple fusion**) to form the **primary endosperm nucleus**. This is unique to angiosperms.

nodes.label: Triple fusion: male gamete + two polar nuclei

visual.alt: Flow of double fertilisation giving zygote and primary endosperm nucleus

slides.narration: Two fusions occur in one embryo sac. Syngamy joins one male gamete with the egg to form the zygote. Triple fusion joins the other male gamete with the two polar nuclei to make the primary endosperm nucleus, which grows into the nutritive endosperm. Together they are called double fertilisation.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: chromosome numbers in double fertilisation
slides.body_md: In an angiosperm the egg cell has 12 chromosomes. Find the number in the zygote and in the primary endosperm nucleus.
bullets: Egg and male gamete are haploid, each 12.
Zygote (syngamy, 2 nuclei): $12 + 12 = 24$ chromosomes.
PEN (triple fusion, 3 nuclei): $12 \times 3 = 36$ chromosomes, so the endosperm is triploid.

visual.alt: Worked table: zygote 24 chromosomes, primary endosperm nucleus 36

slides.narration: Syngamy joins two haploid nuclei, so the zygote is diploid, with twenty four chromosomes. Triple fusion joins three haploid nuclei, so the endosperm nucleus is triploid, with thirty six chromosomes.

slides.body_md: How many nuclei take part in triple fusion?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: pollen and ovules
slides.body_md: An ovary has 30 ovules. Each ovule is fertilised by one pollen tube, and each tube carries 2 male gametes. How many pollen tubes, male gametes and seeds result? How many meiotic divisions make 100 pollen grains?
bullets: Pollen tubes: one per ovule, so 30.
Male gametes: $30 \times 2 = 60$.
Seeds: one per fertilised ovule, so 30.
100 pollen grains need $100 \div 4 = 25$ meiotic divisions of pollen mother cells.

visual.alt: Worked table: 30 tubes, 60 male gametes, 30 seeds, 25 meiotic divisions

slides.narration: Thirty ovules need thirty pollen tubes, each carrying two male gametes, so sixty in all. Each fertilised ovule becomes one seed. Because each pollen mother cell gives four pollen grains, one hundred grains need twenty five meiotic divisions.

slides.heading: Comparing the five groups
slides.body_md: Water for fertilisation is lost with the **seed habit**; vascular tissue appears with **pteridophytes**; fruits are found only in **angiosperms**.

visual.alt: Table comparing the five plant groups on vascular tissue, seeds, fruit, water for fertilisation and dominant phase

slides.narration: Algae and bryophytes lack vascular tissue. Pteridophytes are the first vascular plants but have no seeds. Gymnosperms have naked seeds, and angiosperms have seeds inside fruits. Seed plants no longer need free water for fertilisation because the pollen tube carries the male gametes.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Gymnosperms: naked seeds, heterosporous, pollen grain and female gametophyte kept on the sporophyte; Cycas, Pinus.
Angiosperms: flowers and fruits; dicots (two cotyledons) and monocots (one).
Embryo sac: 7 cells, 8 nuclei.
Double fertilisation: syngamy (zygote) and triple fusion (PEN, triploid endosperm).
Seed plants are diplontic with a dominant sporophyte.

notes.title: Plant Kingdom — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Algae, bryophytes and pteridophytes
sections.body_md:
**Classification of plants.** Early **artificial** systems used a few gross characters (habit, colour, number and shape of leaves; structure of the androecium). **Natural** systems use natural affinities, including internal features such as ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology and phytochemistry. **Phylogenetic** systems use evolutionary relationships. Numerical taxonomy (many characters, computers), cytotaxonomy (chromosome number, structure, behaviour) and chemotaxonomy (chemical constituents) are modern aids. The plant kingdom is divided into five groups: algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.

**Algae** are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and largely aquatic organisms (fresh water, brackish water, sea water, moist stones, soil and wood). The body may be unicellular (*Chlamydomonas*), colonial (*Volvox*), filamentous (*Ulothrix*, *Spirogyra*) or massive (kelps). **Vegetative** reproduction is by fragmentation; **asexual** reproduction by flagellated **zoospores**; **sexual** reproduction by fusion of gametes, which may be isogamous (similar, flagellated or non-flagellated gametes), anisogamous (dissimilar in size) or oogamous (a large non-motile female gamete and a smaller motile male gamete). Algae fix about half of the total carbon dioxide fixed by photosynthesis on Earth and increase the dissolved oxygen of their habitat. Many marine forms (*Porphyra*, *Laminaria*, *Sargassum*) are eaten; **agar** (from *Gelidium* and *Gracilaria*) and **algin** and **carrageen** are used commercially; *Chlorella* and *Spirulina* are protein-rich food supplements.

| Class | Pigments | Stored food | Cell wall | Flagella of motile cells | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Chlorophyceae** (green) | chlorophyll a, b | starch (in pyrenoids) | cellulose | 2–8, equal, apical | *Chlamydomonas*, *Volvox*, *Ulothrix*, *Spirogyra*, *Chara* |
| **Phaeophyceae** (brown) | chlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthin | laminarin, mannitol | cellulose with algin | 2, unequal, lateral | *Ectocarpus*, *Dictyota*, *Laminaria*, *Sargassum*, *Fucus* |
| **Rhodophyceae** (red) | chlorophyll a, d, r-phycoerythrin | floridean starch | cellulose, pectin, polysulphate esters | absent | *Polysiphonia*, *Porphyra*, *Gracilaria*, *Gelidium* |

Brown algae show the greatest variety of body form, from filaments to large kelps with a **holdfast**, **stipe** and **frond**. Red algae are mostly marine, found in warmer areas and at great depths where little light penetrates; they reproduce by non-motile spores and sexually by oogamy. (Habitat wording and pigment lists follow the NCERT table; some references add further minor pigments.)

**Bryophytes** are the amphibians of the plant kingdom: they live in soil but depend on **water for sexual reproduction**, in damp, humid, shaded places. The plant body is a thallus-like or leafy **gametophyte** (haploid, dominant), attached by unicellular or multicellular **rhizoids**; there are no true roots, stems or leaves. The sex organs are the **antheridium** (producing biflagellate antherozoids) and the flask-shaped **archegonium** (one egg). The antherozoids swim in water to the archegonium and the zygote grows into a **sporophyte** of **foot, seta and capsule**, which is not free-living but depends on the gametophyte; meiosis in the capsule makes haploid spores. **Liverworts** (*Marchantia*) have a flat, dorsiventral thallus, reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation and by **gemmae** in gemma cups. **Mosses** (*Funaria*, *Polytrichum*, *Sphagnum*) have a creeping green **protonema** stage that develops from a spore and an upright, leafy stage, with multicellular branched rhizoids; vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation and budding in the secondary protonema. *Sphagnum* gives **peat** (fuel) and, because it holds water, packing material for living plants; mosses with lichens colonise rocks and prevent soil erosion.

**Pteridophytes** (ferns, horsetails, club mosses) are the first terrestrial plants with **vascular tissue** (xylem and phloem). They grow in cool, damp, shady places. The main plant body is the **sporophyte** with true root, stem and leaves; leaves are small (**microphylls**, *Selaginella*) or large (**macrophylls**, ferns). Sporangia are borne on **sporophylls**, sometimes in cones (**strobili**: *Selaginella*, *Equisetum*). Meiosis of spore mother cells makes spores, which germinate into a small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic **prothallus** (gametophyte) bearing antheridia and archegonia. Water is needed for the antherozoids to reach the egg, which limits their spread. The zygote grows into the dominant sporophyte. Most are **homosporous**; *Selaginella* and *Salvinia* are **heterosporous** (macrospores and microspores), and the female gametophyte is retained on the parent sporophyte, where the zygote begins to develop — a precursor of the **seed habit**. Classes: Psilopsida (*Psilotum*), Lycopsida (*Selaginella*, *Lycopodium*), Sphenopsida (*Equisetum*), Pteropsida (*Dryopteris*, *Pteris*, *Adiantum*).

**Alternation of generations.** Sexual reproduction in plants involves a haploid **gametophyte** that makes gametes and a diploid **sporophyte** that makes spores by meiosis. In the **haplontic** pattern the dominant, free-living body is the haploid gametophyte and the sporophyte is only the one-celled zygote, which divides by meiosis (*Volvox*, *Spirogyra*, some *Chlamydomonas*). In the **diplontic** pattern the diploid sporophyte is dominant and the gametophyte is a few cells (all gymnosperms and angiosperms; the alga *Fucus*). In the **haplo-diplontic** pattern both phases are multicellular and free-living (bryophytes, where the gametophyte dominates; pteridophytes, where the sporophyte dominates; some algae such as *Ectocarpus*, *Polysiphonia* and kelps).

*Counting rule used in questions:* one diploid spore mother cell gives four haploid spores by meiosis.

sections.heading: 2. Gymnosperms and angiosperms
sections.body_md:
**Gymnosperms** (*gymnos*, naked; *sperma*, seed) have **ovules that are not enclosed by an ovary wall**, so the seeds are naked after fertilisation. They include medium-sized or tall trees and shrubs; the giant redwood *Sequoia* is among the tallest trees. The roots are **tap roots**; in *Pinus* roots have a fungal association (**mycorrhiza**), and in *Cycas* small **coralloid roots** associate with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. Stems are unbranched (*Cycas*) or branched (*Pinus*, *Cedrus*). Leaves are simple or compound: the pinnate leaves of *Cycas* last for a few years, and in conifers needle-like leaves, a thick cuticle and sunken stomata reduce water loss.

Gymnosperms are **heterosporous**. Microspores and megaspores are produced in sporangia borne on sporophylls arranged spirally on an axis to form **cones (strobili)**. The **male (microsporangiate) cone** bears microsporophylls and microsporangia; the microspores develop into a very reduced male gametophyte, the **pollen grain**. The **female (macrosporangiate) cone** bears megasporophylls with **ovules**; the nucellus is protected by envelopes, and the whole is the ovule. One cell of the nucellus becomes the **megaspore mother cell**, which divides by meiosis into four megaspores; one develops into the multicellular female gametophyte with two or more **archegonia**. Male and female cones may be on the same tree (*Pinus*) or on different trees (*Cycas*). Unlike bryophytes and pteridophytes, the gametophytes of gymnosperms are **not free-living**; they stay within the sporangia on the sporophyte. Pollen is carried by air currents to the ovule opening, and a **pollen tube** carries the male gametes to the archegonia. After fertilisation the zygote becomes an embryo and the ovule a **seed**, which is not covered.

**Angiosperms** are flowering plants. Pollen grains and ovules develop in the **flower**, and seeds are **enclosed in fruits**. They range from the minute *Wolffia* to *Eucalyptus* trees over 100 metres tall, and provide food, fodder, fuel, medicines and many commercial products. There are two classes: **dicotyledons** (two cotyledons in the seed, reticulate venation, tetramerous or pentamerous flowers) and **monocotyledons** (one cotyledon, parallel venation, trimerous flowers). The male organ is the **stamen** (filament and anther, with pollen grains); the female organ is the **pistil** or carpel (stigma, style, ovary with ovules). The female gametophyte is the **embryo sac**: **7 cells and 8 nuclei** — an egg apparatus (one egg and two synergids) at the micropylar end, three antipodal cells at the other end, and a large central cell with two polar nuclei. The male gametophyte is the pollen grain, which germinates on the stigma into a pollen tube that carries two male gametes into the embryo sac.

**Double fertilisation.** One male gamete fuses with the egg (**syngamy**) to form the diploid **zygote**; the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (**triple fusion**) to form the triploid **primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)**. Because two fusions occur in one embryo sac, this is called double fertilisation, an event unique to flowering plants. The zygote develops into the embryo and the PEN into the endosperm; the ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes the fruit. Angiosperms are **diplontic**: the sporophyte is dominant.

**Comparison.** Gymnosperms: naked seeds, no flowers or fruits, no embryo sac. Angiosperms: flowers, fruits, embryo sac, double fertilisation and triploid endosperm. Both have a dominant sporophyte, are heterosporous and do not need free water for fertilisation because a pollen tube carries the male gametes.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving chlorophyll b to brown or red algae (only green algae have it; brown have fucoxanthin, red have phycoerythrin).
- Calling the moss plant a sporophyte (the green leafy plant is the gametophyte; the sporophyte is the capsule on a seta).
- Saying pteridophytes have seeds, or that bryophytes have xylem and phloem.
- Confusing homosporous with heterosporous, or calling Cycas coralloid roots "nodules of bacteria" (the partners are cyanobacteria).
- Describing the endosperm of angiosperms as diploid (it is triploid).
- Writing that gymnosperms have fruits or flowers.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a pigment or stored food; a class of algae; a part of the moss or fern; which generation dominates.
- 2–3-mark answers: three classes of algae; features of bryophytes or pteridophytes; haplontic versus diplontic; gymnosperm features; dicot versus monocot; double fertilisation.
- 5-mark answers: algae classes with examples; life cycle of a bryophyte or pteridophyte; gymnosperms versus angiosperms; embryo sac and double fertilisation.
- Counting items: spores from mother cells, chromosome numbers in zygote and PEN, male gametes needed — show the working.

cards.front_md: Name the five groups of the plant kingdom.
cards.back_md: Algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms.

cards.front_md: What basis does a phylogenetic system use?
cards.back_md: Evolutionary relationships among organisms.
Chlorophyll a and b.
Chlorophyll a, c and fucoxanthin.

cards.front_md: Pigment that makes red algae red?
cards.back_md: r-phycoerythrin.

cards.front_md: Stored food of green, brown and red algae?
cards.back_md: Starch; laminarin and mannitol; floridean starch.

cards.front_md: Three parts of a large brown alga?
cards.back_md: Holdfast, stipe and frond.
Agar (red algae), algin (brown algae), carrageen; Chlorella and Spirulina as food supplements.

cards.front_md: Three kinds of sexual reproduction in algae?
cards.back_md: Isogamous, anisogamous, oogamous.

cards.front_md: Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom?
cards.back_md: They live on land but need water for fertilisation.
The haploid gametophyte.
Foot, seta and capsule.
Green multicellular asexual buds formed in gemma cups of liverworts.

cards.front_md: Two stages of a moss gametophyte?
cards.back_md: Protonema stage, then the leafy stage.
Peat as fuel; packing material for living plants (holds water).

cards.front_md: Why are pteridophytes the first vascular plants?
cards.back_md: They are the first terrestrial plants to have xylem and phloem.
Prothallus: small, free-living, photosynthetic.
One kind of spore; two kinds (macrospores and microspores), as in Selaginella and Salvinia.

cards.front_md: Four classes of pteridophytes with an example each?
cards.back_md: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), Pteropsida (Dryopteris).
Dominant haploid gametophyte; the zygote is the only diploid cell; e.g. Spirogyra.
Dominant diploid sporophyte; gametophyte of a few cells; e.g. gymnosperms, angiosperms, Fucus.
Both phases multicellular and free-living; bryophytes, pteridophytes, kelps.

cards.front_md: How many spores from one spore mother cell?
cards.back_md: Four haploid spores by meiosis.
Naked seed: ovules are not enclosed by an ovary wall.
Coralloid roots (nitrogen fixation); Pinus has mycorrhiza.
Needle shape, thick cuticle, sunken stomata: less water loss.
The very reduced male gametophyte, formed from a microspore.
Two versus one cotyledon; reticulate versus parallel venation; 4 or 5 versus 3 floral parts.
7 cells, 8 nuclei: egg and 2 synergids, 3 antipodals, central cell with 2 polar nuclei.
Syngamy (zygote) plus triple fusion (primary endosperm nucleus, triploid); unique to angiosperms.

questions.stem_md: A marine biologist collects an olive-brown alga from a rocky shore. It is anchored by a holdfast and stores mannitol. Which pigment is mainly responsible for its colour?
questions.solution_md: Brown algae (Phaeophyceae) have chlorophyll a, c and the brown xanthophyll fucoxanthin and store laminarin and mannitol — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Cells of a freshwater filamentous alga contain bodies called pyrenoids that turn blue-black with iodine. Which food reserve and class does this indicate?
questions.solution_md: Green algae store starch in pyrenoids; floridean starch belongs to red algae, laminarin and mannitol to brown algae — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A food-technology student wants to extract agar for a laboratory culture medium. Which alga should she harvest?
questions.solution_md: Agar is obtained from the red algae Gelidium and Gracilaria; algin comes from brown algae — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Under a microscope a student sees a pear-shaped motile cell with two unequal flagella attached to its side. Which kind of alga most probably released it?

options.text_md: A red alga, which has no motile cells
A diatom-like green alga with no flagella

questions.solution_md: Brown algae have two unequal, laterally attached flagella on their motile cells; green algae have two to eight equal apical flagella and red algae have none — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Algae are important to the whole planet because they

options.text_md: fix almost all the carbon dioxide taken up by photosynthesis on Earth
fix about half of the total carbon dioxide taken up by photosynthesis on Earth
fix only about a tenth of the carbon dioxide taken up by photosynthesis
release carbon dioxide but never oxygen into water

questions.solution_md: Algae carry out about half of the total carbon dioxide fixation on Earth and raise the dissolved oxygen of their surroundings — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the drawing of a brown alga, which part anchors the alga to the rock, and what is it called?
questions.solution_md: C is the branched root-like holdfast; B is the stipe (stalk) and A the frond (blade) — option (d).

questions.solution_md: Chlorophyll b and starch mark the green algae (Chlorophyceae), which include Spirogyra — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Bryophytes are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom because they

options.text_md: spend half of their life under water and half in air
live in soil and on land but need water to complete sexual reproduction
have gills like some animals when they are young
have two kinds of vascular tissue, xylem and phloem

questions.solution_md: Bryophytes grow on land but the antherozoids must swim in water to reach the egg — option (b).

questions.stem_md: On a damp garden wall a student finds a flat green thallus with small cups, each holding tiny green discs. These cups and discs are most probably

options.text_md: gemma cups and gemmae of a liverwort, used for asexual reproduction
antheridia and archegonia of a moss, used for sexual reproduction
sori and sporangia of a fern, used for spore dispersal
coralloid roots of a cycad, used for nitrogen fixation

questions.solution_md: Liverworts such as Marchantia produce green multicellular buds, gemmae, in gemma cups on the thallus; they detach and grow into new individuals — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A moss spore lands on moist soil and grows into a creeping, green, branched, thread-like stage. This stage is the
questions.solution_md: In mosses a spore develops directly into the creeping green protonema; the prothallus belongs to pteridophytes — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the drawing of a moss plant, in which marked part does meiosis produce the spores?
questions.solution_md: The capsule (A) at the top of the sporophyte makes haploid spores by meiosis; B is the seta, D the leaf-like flaps and E the rhizoids — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A nursery packs live seedlings in moist moss before sending them by lorry, and a village burns dried moss deposits from a bog as fuel. The moss in both cases is

options.text_md: Funaria, which holds a great deal of water and forms peat
Marchantia, which holds a great deal of water and forms coal
Sphagnum, which has vascular tissue and forms coal
Sphagnum, which holds a great deal of water and forms peat

questions.solution_md: Sphagnum provides peat used as fuel, and its water-holding capacity makes it a packing material for living plants — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In which plant is the gametophyte the dominant, independent phase, with the sporophyte depending on it?
questions.solution_md: In bryophytes such as the moss Funaria the sporophyte is attached to and nourished by the gametophyte; in ferns, Selaginella and pine the sporophyte dominates — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which feature do pteridophytes have that bryophytes lack?

options.text_md: A gametophyte that needs water for fertilisation
Spores produced by meiosis in sporangia
Antheridia and archegonia as sex organs
Xylem and phloem in a sporophyte with true roots, stem and leaves

questions.solution_md: Pteridophytes are the first terrestrial plants with vascular tissue; the other three features are shared with bryophytes — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the drawing of a fern sporophyte, which marked part is a cluster of sporangia?
questions.solution_md: C is the sorus, a cluster of sporangia on the underside of a pinna; A is the frond, B a pinna and F the roots — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A forester finds a small, heart-shaped, green, free-living plant on a damp shady forest floor beneath ferns. It bears antheridia and archegonia. This plant is

options.text_md: the prothallus, the haploid gametophyte of a fern
a young fern sporophyte, which is diploid
a protonema of a moss, which is diploid
the embryo sac of a flowering plant

questions.solution_md: The prothallus is the small, multicellular, free-living, photosynthetic gametophyte of pteridophytes and bears the sex organs — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In Selaginella and Salvinia the female gametophyte is retained on the parent sporophyte and the zygote starts to develop inside it. Why is this event important in plant evolution?

options.text_md: It is a precursor of the seed habit
It shows that these plants have no spores
It removes the need for any gametophyte

questions.solution_md: Retention of the female gametophyte and development of the zygote into an embryo on the parent are a step towards the seed habit — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The body of an alga is diploid, and only its gametes are haploid. Which life-cycle pattern does it follow, and which alga is an example?
questions.solution_md: A dominant diploid body with haploid gametes is the diplontic pattern, seen in Fucus; Volvox and Spirogyra are haplontic — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a pond alga the cells are haploid, and the zygote divides by meiosis to form four haploid cells. Its life-cycle pattern is
questions.solution_md: Only the zygote is diploid and it divides by meiosis, so the pattern is haplontic (as in Spirogyra) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The prothallus of a fern is a diploid plant on which the sori are borne.
questions.solution_md: False. The prothallus is the haploid gametophyte with antheridia and archegonia; sori are borne on the diploid sporophyte.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a moss, the protonema develops directly from a spore.
questions.solution_md: True. The spore germinates into the creeping, green, branched protonema, which later gives the leafy stage.

questions.stem_md: Green, multicellular asexual buds that develop in gemma cups on the thallus of a liverwort are called ______.
questions.solution_md: Gemmae.

questions.solution_md: Zoospores.

questions.stem_md: Match each structure (column I) with the plant group in which it is found (column II).
questions.solution_md: Gemma cups are liverwort structures, sori belong to ferns, coralloid roots to Cycas and the embryo sac to angiosperms.

questions.stem_md: A moss capsule contains 40 spore mother cells. Assuming that every cell completes meiosis, how many spores does the capsule release?
questions.solution_md: Each spore mother cell gives 4 spores: $40 \times 4 = 160$.

questions.stem_md: A fern sorus has 25 sporangia and each sporangium holds 16 spore mother cells. How many spores can one sorus release?
questions.solution_md: Spore mother cells: $25 \times 16 = 400$. Each gives 4 spores: $400 \times 4 = 1600$.

A botany club lists twelve plants it found on a field trip.

| Plant | Group |

| Marchantia | bryophyte |
| Funaria | bryophyte |
| Sphagnum | bryophyte |
| Selaginella | pteridophyte |
| Equisetum | pteridophyte |

How many of these twelve plants have vascular tissue (xylem and phloem)?
questions.solution_md: Pteridophytes (3), gymnosperms (2) and angiosperms (2) have vascular tissue: $3 + 2 + 2 = 7$. Bryophytes and algae have none.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an artificial and a natural system of plant classification, with one feature used in each.

answer.model_answer_md: An **artificial** system uses a few easily seen gross characters, such as **habit, colour, or the number and shape of leaves**. A **natural** system uses **natural affinities** among organisms, including **internal features** such as ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology and phytochemistry, so related plants are grouped together.

questions.solution_md: Artificial: few gross characters; natural: many characters including internal ones.

marking_scheme.step: Artificial: few gross characters with an example
Natural: natural affinities with an example

questions.stem_md: Why are bryophytes called the amphibians of the plant kingdom? Name their two classes.

answer.model_answer_md: Bryophytes **live on land** in damp, shaded places, but they **depend on water for sexual reproduction**, because the biflagellate antherozoids must swim to the egg in the archegonium. Their two classes are **liverworts and mosses**.

questions.solution_md: Land habit, water needed; liverworts and mosses.

marking_scheme.step: Land-living but water needed for fertilisation

questions.stem_md: A student sees a liverwort thallus dotted with cups holding green discs. Name these structures and explain how they help the plant.

answer.model_answer_md: They are **gemma cups** holding **gemmae**, which are green, multicellular **asexual buds**. A gemma **detaches from the parent** and **germinates into a new thallus**, so the liverwort multiplies without gametes or fertilisation.

questions.solution_md: Gemmae in gemma cups: asexual reproduction.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between homosporous and heterosporous pteridophytes, with one example of the second kind.

answer.model_answer_md: In **homosporous** plants all the spores are of **one kind**, as in most ferns. **Heterosporous** plants produce **two kinds of spores**, large **megaspores** and small **microspores**, which grow into female and male gametophytes; examples are **Selaginella** and **Salvinia**.

questions.solution_md: One kind versus two kinds of spores; Selaginella.

questions.stem_md: What is a prothallus, and why does its need for water and shade limit the spread of ferns?

answer.model_answer_md: The **prothallus** is the small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic **gametophyte** of a pteridophyte, bearing antheridia and archegonia. It needs **cool, damp, shady places** to grow, and **water for the antherozoids to reach the egg**, so ferns are restricted to narrow geographical regions.

questions.solution_md: Gametophyte; damp shade and water needed.

marking_scheme.step: Water and shade needed, limiting spread

questions.stem_md: Explain how heterospory in Selaginella can be seen as a step towards the seed habit.

answer.model_answer_md: In Selaginella **megaspores and microspores** grow into **female and male gametophytes**. The **female gametophyte is retained on the parent sporophyte**, and the **zygote develops into a young embryo inside it**. Keeping the embryo on the parent in this way is a **precursor of the seed habit**.

questions.solution_md: Retained female gametophyte and embryo development: seed habit.

marking_scheme.step: Embryo develops inside; precursor of seed

questions.stem_md: Name two commercial products obtained from algae, with the class of alga that yields each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Agar**, used in culture media and food, is obtained from the **red algae** *Gelidium* and *Gracilaria*. **Algin**, a water-holding hydrocolloid, is obtained from **brown algae**. (Carrageen from red algae is another example.)

questions.solution_md: Agar from red algae; algin from brown algae.

questions.stem_md: A pine tree thrives on a cold, windy slope where water is scarce in winter. Name two features of its leaves that help it and say how.

answer.model_answer_md: Pine leaves are **needle-like**, which **reduces the surface area** exposed to wind and sun. They also have a **thick cuticle** and **sunken stomata**, which further **reduce loss of water** by transpiration, so the tree survives extremes of temperature, humidity and wind.

questions.solution_md: Needle shape, thick cuticle, sunken stomata reduce water loss.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between dicotyledons and monocotyledons, with one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Dicots** have **two cotyledons** in the seed and **reticulate venation** in leaves, with flowers of four or five parts (pea, mustard). **Monocots** have **one cotyledon** and **parallel venation**, with flowers of three parts (wheat, maize).

questions.solution_md: Cotyledons and venation, with examples.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of a mature angiosperm embryo sac, giving the number of cells and nuclei.

answer.model_answer_md: The embryo sac has **7 cells and 8 nuclei**. At the micropylar end is the **egg apparatus** of one **egg cell and two synergids**; at the other end are **three antipodal cells**; and the large **central cell** contains **two polar nuclei**.

questions.solution_md: Seven cells, eight nuclei; arrangement.

marking_scheme.step: Egg apparatus, antipodals, central cell with polar nuclei

questions.stem_md: Distinguish green, brown and red algae on the basis of their pigments and stored food.

answer.model_answer_md: **Green algae** have **chlorophyll a and b** and store **starch** in pyrenoids. **Brown algae** have **chlorophyll a and c** and the brown pigment **fucoxanthin**, and store **laminarin and mannitol**. **Red algae** have **chlorophyll a and d** and the red pigment **r-phycoerythrin**, and store **floridean starch**.

questions.solution_md: Pigments and food reserves of the three classes.

marking_scheme.step: Brown: chlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthin; laminarin, mannitol
Red: chlorophyll a, d, phycoerythrin; floridean starch

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the haplontic and diplontic life cycles, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: In the **haplontic** cycle the dominant, free-living body is the **haploid gametophyte**, and the sporophyte is only the **one-celled zygote**, which divides by meiosis; examples are **Volvox and Spirogyra**. In the **diplontic** cycle the **diploid sporophyte** is dominant and the gametophyte is reduced to a few cells; examples are **gymnosperms, angiosperms and the alga Fucus**.

questions.solution_md: Dominant phase and zygote or gametophyte in each.

marking_scheme.step: Haplontic: haploid dominant, zygote only diploid; example
Diplontic: diploid dominant, gametophyte few cells; example

questions.stem_md: A student pulls a moss plant from a wall and notices a thin stalk topped by a small capsule growing from its tip. Which generation does each part belong to, how are they related and what happens in the capsule?

answer.model_answer_md: The **leafy shoot with rhizoids** is the **haploid gametophyte**. The **foot, seta and capsule** form the **diploid sporophyte**, which grows from the zygote, is **attached to the gametophyte** and **depends on it for nutrition**. In the capsule, cells undergo **meiosis** to make **haploid spores**, which germinate into a protonema.

questions.solution_md: Gametophyte and sporophyte parts, dependence, meiosis in capsule.

marking_scheme.step: Leafy shoot is gametophyte; foot, seta, capsule are sporophyte

questions.stem_md: Describe how the male and female gametophytes of a gymnosperm are formed and where they live.

answer.model_answer_md: In the **male cone**, microsporangia produce **microspores**, which develop into the very reduced male gametophyte, the **pollen grain**. In the **female cone**, a **megaspore mother cell** of the ovule divides by meiosis into **four megaspores**; one becomes the multicellular **female gametophyte** with **archegonia**. Neither is free-living: both stay **within the sporangia on the sporophyte**.

questions.solution_md: Microspore to pollen grain; megaspore to female gametophyte; not free-living.

marking_scheme.step: Megaspore mother cell, four megaspores, one gametophyte with archegonia

questions.stem_md: What is double fertilisation? Name its two events and the product and ploidy of each.

answer.model_answer_md: In **double fertilisation** two fusions occur in one embryo sac. **Syngamy** is the fusion of a male gamete with the **egg**, giving the **diploid zygote**, which becomes the embryo. **Triple fusion** is the fusion of the other male gamete with the **two polar nuclei**, giving the **triploid primary endosperm nucleus**, which becomes the endosperm. It is unique to **flowering plants**.

questions.solution_md: Syngamy and triple fusion with products and ploidy.

marking_scheme.step: Definition: two fusions in one embryo sac

questions.stem_md: State three differences between gymnosperms and angiosperms.

answer.model_answer_md: **Gymnosperms** have **naked ovules and seeds**, with no flower or fruit, and no embryo sac. **Angiosperms** have **flowers**, with ovules enclosed in an **ovary** that becomes a **fruit** enclosing the seeds; they have a seven-celled **embryo sac**. In angiosperms **double fertilisation** forms a **triploid endosperm**, which gymnosperms lack.

questions.solution_md: Naked versus enclosed seeds; flowers and fruits; double fertilisation.

marking_scheme.step: Naked versus enclosed ovules and seeds
Flower and fruit only in angiosperms
Embryo sac and double fertilisation only in angiosperms

questions.stem_md: Describe the main plant body of a fern and the way its spores give rise to the next generation.

answer.model_answer_md: The main plant body is the **diploid sporophyte** with **true root, stem and leaves** and vascular tissue. **Sporangia** on the leaves make spores by **meiosis in spore mother cells**. A spore germinates into a small, free-living, haploid **prothallus** that bears **antheridia and archegonia**. After fertilisation in water the **zygote** grows into a new sporophyte.

questions.solution_md: Sporophyte, spores by meiosis, prothallus, zygote.

marking_scheme.step: Sporophyte with true organs and vascular tissue

questions.stem_md: Describe the three classes of algae, comparing their pigments, stored food, cell wall, habitat and examples, and mention two ways in which algae are useful to humans.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Chlorophyceae (green algae)** have chlorophyll a and b, store starch in pyrenoids, have cellulose walls and live in fresh, brackish and salt water; examples are *Chlamydomonas*, *Volvox*, *Spirogyra* and *Chara*.

**Phaeophyceae (brown algae)** have chlorophyll a and c and fucoxanthin, store laminarin and mannitol, have cellulose walls with an algin coating and live mainly in brackish and salt water; examples are *Laminaria*, *Sargassum* and *Fucus*. Their body shows a holdfast, stipe and frond.

**Rhodophyceae (red algae)** have chlorophyll a and d and r-phycoerythrin, store floridean starch, have walls of cellulose, pectin and polysulphate esters, are mostly marine, in warmer areas and at great depths, and have no flagella; examples are *Polysiphonia*, *Porphyra*, *Gracilaria* and *Gelidium*.

**Uses.** Algae fix about half the carbon dioxide taken up in photosynthesis, adding oxygen to water; agar comes from *Gelidium* and *Gracilaria*, and *Chlorella* and *Spirulina* are protein-rich food supplements.

questions.solution_md: Three classes compared; two uses.

questions.stem_md: Describe the general features of bryophytes, compare liverworts with mosses, and explain their life cycle and their importance.

answer.model_answer_md:
**General features.** Bryophytes live in damp, shaded places and need water for fertilisation. The plant body is a haploid gametophyte, thallus-like or leafy, without true roots, stem or leaves, anchored by rhizoids. The antheridium makes biflagellate antherozoids and the flask-shaped archegonium one egg.

**Liverworts and mosses.** A liverwort such as *Marchantia* has a flat, dorsiventral thallus and reproduces asexually by fragmentation and by gemmae in gemma cups. A moss such as *Funaria* has a creeping protonema that grows from a spore and an upright leafy stage with spirally arranged leaves and branched rhizoids; it multiplies by fragmentation and budding.

**Life cycle.** Antherozoids swim to the egg; the zygote grows into a sporophyte of foot, seta and capsule, which depends on the gametophyte. Meiosis in the capsule makes haploid spores that grow into new gametophytes.

**Importance.** *Sphagnum* gives peat and a packing material; mosses and lichens colonise bare rock, helping succession, and mats of moss reduce soil erosion.

questions.solution_md: Features, liverwort versus moss, life cycle, importance.

questions.stem_md: Explain why pteridophytes are called the first vascular land plants. Describe their sporophyte and gametophyte, the four classes, and the significance of heterospory.

answer.model_answer_md:
**First vascular plants.** Pteridophytes are the first terrestrial plants with xylem and phloem, which move water and food through a sporophyte with true roots, stem and leaves, small (microphylls, *Selaginella*) or large (macrophylls, ferns).

**Sporophyte and gametophyte.** The sporophyte is dominant. Sporangia on sporophylls, sometimes in strobili as in *Selaginella* and *Equisetum*, make spores by meiosis of spore mother cells. A spore grows into a small, free-living, photosynthetic prothallus with antheridia and archegonia. It needs cool, damp, shady places and water for the antherozoids, which restricts spread. The zygote grows into the sporophyte.

**Classes.** Psilopsida (*Psilotum*), Lycopsida (*Selaginella*, *Lycopodium*), Sphenopsida (*Equisetum*) and Pteropsida (*Dryopteris*, *Pteris*, *Adiantum*).

**Heterospory.** *Selaginella* and *Salvinia* make megaspores and microspores; the female gametophyte is kept on the parent and the zygote begins to develop in it, a precursor of the seed habit.

questions.solution_md: Vascular tissue; sporophyte and prothallus; classes; heterospory.

marking_scheme.step: Sporangia, spores and prothallus; limits on spread

questions.stem_md: Explain alternation of generations in plants. Distinguish the haplontic, diplontic and haplo-diplontic patterns, and place the bryophytes, pteridophytes and seed plants among them with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Alternation.** A haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis; their fusion gives a diploid zygote that grows into a sporophyte; the sporophyte makes haploid spores by meiosis, and the spores grow into new gametophytes.

**Haplontic.** The dominant, free-living body is the haploid gametophyte. The sporophyte is only the one-celled zygote, which divides by meiosis. Examples: *Volvox*, *Spirogyra*.

**Diplontic.** The diploid sporophyte is dominant, independent and photosynthetic, and the gametophyte is a few cells. Examples: *Fucus*, gymnosperms and angiosperms.

**Haplo-diplontic.** Both phases are multicellular and free-living, as in *Ectocarpus* and kelps.

**Placing the groups.** Bryophytes and pteridophytes are haplo-diplontic, because both a gametophyte and a sporophyte are multicellular and the two alternate; in bryophytes the gametophyte dominates, and in pteridophytes the sporophyte does. Seed plants are diplontic: the sporophyte dominates and the gametophytes are tiny and kept on it.

questions.solution_md: Alternation; three patterns; placing the groups.

marking_scheme.step: Placing bryophytes, pteridophytes, seed plants with reasons

questions.stem_md: Describe the general features of gymnosperms, with examples, and explain how the male and female gametophytes are formed and how fertilisation leads to a seed.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Features.** Gymnosperms bear ovules that are not enclosed by an ovary wall, so their seeds are naked. They are medium to tall trees and shrubs (*Sequoia* is among the tallest). Roots are tap roots, with mycorrhiza in *Pinus* and coralloid roots with cyanobacteria in *Cycas*. Stems are unbranched (*Cycas*) or branched (*Pinus*, *Cedrus*). Leaves are pinnate in *Cycas* and needle-like in conifers, with a thick cuticle and sunken stomata that cut water loss.

**Gametophytes.** Gymnosperms are heterosporous. Microspores form in male cones and develop into pollen grains, a reduced male gametophyte. In ovules of female cones a megaspore mother cell divides by meiosis into four megaspores; one forms the female gametophyte with archegonia. Cones may be on the same tree (*Pinus*) or on different trees (*Cycas*). The gametophytes are not free-living.

**Seed.** Pollen is carried by air to the ovule; the pollen tube delivers the male gametes to the archegonium. The zygote becomes an embryo and the ovule a naked seed.

questions.solution_md: Features; gametophytes; fertilisation and seed.

marking_scheme.step: Naked seeds and body features with examples

questions.stem_md: Describe the angiosperms: the two classes with distinguishing features, the male and female organs of the flower, the structure of the embryo sac, and double fertilisation with its products.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Angiosperms** bear pollen grains and ovules in flowers and have seeds enclosed in fruits. **Dicots** have two cotyledons, reticulate venation and flowers of four or five parts; **monocots** have one cotyledon, parallel venation and flowers of three parts.

**Flower.** The male organ is the stamen, with a filament and an anther holding pollen grains. The female organ is the pistil, with stigma, style and an ovary containing ovules.

**Embryo sac.** The female gametophyte has 7 cells and 8 nuclei: an egg and two synergids at the micropylar end, three antipodals at the other end, and a central cell with two polar nuclei.

**Double fertilisation.** The pollen tube releases two male gametes. One fuses with the egg (syngamy) to form the diploid zygote; the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (triple fusion) to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus. The zygote becomes the embryo and the nucleus the endosperm; ovules become seeds and the ovary a fruit.

questions.solution_md: Classes; flower; embryo sac; double fertilisation.

questions.stem_md: A student writes: "Vascular tissue and seeds appeared together in plants, so a plant with xylem and phloem always makes seeds, and any plant that lives on land no longer needs water to reproduce." Evaluate this statement using the five plant groups.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Vascular tissue without seeds.** The statement is wrong in its first part. Pteridophytes, such as ferns, *Selaginella* and *Equisetum*, are the first plants with xylem and phloem, but they have no seeds: they reproduce by spores. Seeds appear only in gymnosperms and angiosperms.

**Land plants and water.** The second part is also wrong. Bryophytes live on land, and pteridophytes too, but both need water for the antherozoids to reach the egg, which is why they stay in damp places; a free-living prothallus also needs damp shade. Only seed plants do without free water, because the pollen tube carries the male gametes to the egg.

**Evidence from the groups.** Algae and bryophytes lack vascular tissue; pteridophytes have it but not seeds; gymnosperms have naked seeds; angiosperms have seeds in fruits.

**Judgement.** Vascular tissue came before seeds, and living on land does not by itself end the need for water. Only the seed habit does.

questions.solution_md: Evaluates both claims using the five groups.

marking_scheme.step: Bryophytes and pteridophytes need water; seed plants do not

the whole sporophyte generation of the pine

Parallel venation and flowers with three parts

questions.passage_md: A gardener studies a mango-like flowering tree whose egg cell has 14 chromosomes. Pollen from one flower lands on the stigma of another and a pollen tube grows down the style into an ovule, where it releases two male gametes into the embryo sac. Weeks later the ovary has swollen into a fruit.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) The ovary

**(b)** 42

**(c)** (i) One male gamete **fuses with the egg** (syngamy) to form the **zygote**, and the second **fuses with the two polar nuclei** (triple fusion) to form the **primary endosperm nucleus**. Both fusions need a male gamete, so **two male gametes** are needed.

**OR** (ii) The zygote forms by syngamy, the fusion of two haploid nuclei (the egg and one male gamete), so it has **28 chromosomes** and is diploid. It then divides repeatedly and develops into the **embryo** of the seed.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** After fertilisation the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovules become seeds — option (d).

**(b)** The egg cell is haploid, $n = 14$. The primary endosperm nucleus is triploid: $3 \times 14 = 42$.

**(c)** (i) One for syngamy, one for triple fusion.

(ii) Zygote 28, embryo.
